design_detail: Retrospective multicentre chart review by the Cocaine Associated Myocardial Infarction (CAMI) Study Group at 29 acute-care hospitals in the United States, covering 1987–1993; the authors call it a retrospective cross-sectional survey (p. 1237). Hospital patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction whose initial ECG met TIMI criteria for thrombolysis were split into those who received thrombolytic therapy (n=25) and those who did not (n=41), and in-hospital deaths, complications, cardiac enzyme peaks and clinical signs of reperfusion were compared. The treating clinicians decided who was thrombolysed; the study did not. Filed as a retrospective cohort appraised with ROBINS-I because a hospital treatment is compared between non-randomized groups.
can_establish: That among 25 hospital patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction who were thrombolysed in 1987–1993, none had an intracerebral haemorrhage or bleeding needing transfusion and none died in hospital, and that treated and untreated ECG-eligible patients did not differ significantly in enzyme peaks or in-hospital complications.
cannot_establish: That thrombolysis carries a low risk in this population (0 of 25 is compatible with a major-complication rate of up to about 12–14%); its safety in patients thrombolysed for ST elevation who turned out not to have an infarction (excluded by design); or whether it works (treatment was not randomized, co-treatments differed, and efficacy was judged from chart notes and from enzyme peaks sampled every 8–12 hours).

sample.recruitment: Records (clinic): at 29 acute-care institutions (named in the Acknowledgment, p. 1240), patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction from 1987 to 1993 were found by cross-referencing ICD-9 codes for myocardial infarction with the codes for cocaine and/or drug abuse (the coding categories searched), and by reviewing the records of all patients with infarction aged 40 or younger for evidence of cocaine use (p. 1237, Methods › Patients).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All three criteria were required: (1) cocaine use in the 24 hours before presentation by history, or cocaine metabolites on a urine screen; (2) infarction by both the international diagnostic criteria (ref. 24) and the attending physician's clinical impression; (3) an initial ECG meeting TIMI criteria for thrombolysis (p. 1237). Patients not meeting the ECG criteria were excluded before the comparison (p. 1238).
sample.demographics: Not thrombolysed (n=41) vs thrombolysed (n=25): mean age 38.1 (SD 9.8) vs 39.8 (SD 10.3); men 73% vs 88%; nonwhite 83% vs 64%; hypertension 34% vs 20%; diabetes 7% vs 4%; hypercholesterolaemia 20% vs 20%; family history 34% vs 48%; tobacco 85% vs 96%; previous infarction 10% vs 16% (Table 1, p. 1238).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (record review). Reperfusion information was charted for 21 of the 25 thrombolysed patients (p. 1238).
sample.selection_effects: The number excluded for not meeting the ECG criteria is not given, and whether the 25 and 41 count patients or infarctions is not stated (136 infarctions occurred in 130 patients) (p. 1238). Case-finding relied on coding of cocaine or drug abuse and on chart review limited to patients aged 40 or younger, so older patients and those whose cocaine use was not recorded were less likely to enter. Requiring a confirmed infarction removes patients who were thrombolysed for ST elevation without an infarction, a group the authors say may be large (in one series 43% met TIMI criteria without infarction, p. 1239). Who received thrombolysis was decided by clinicians at 29 hospitals over 7 years, for reasons not recorded.

exposure.measurement: Intervention: thrombolytic therapy as recorded in the chart. The agent and dosing regimen were abstracted (p. 1238) but are not reported; one patient is said to have received streptokinase. Cocaine use: chart history of use within 24 hours or a positive urine screen.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Thrombolytic agents and doses not reported. Time since last cocaine use, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: under 4 hours 39% vs 40%, under 24 hours 81% vs 64%. Duration of chest pain at presentation: under 1 hour 20% vs 28%, 1–3 hours 34% vs 48%, 3–6 hours 12% vs 12%, 6–24 hours 20% vs 8%, over 24 hours 5% vs 4%, unknown 2% vs 0%; three untreated patients had no chest pain (Table 1, p. 1238). Route of cocaine use was abstracted but not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded or reported, apart from tobacco (85% vs 96%).

comparison.controls: 41 hospital patients with cocaine-associated infarction whose initial ECG met TIMI criteria but who were not thrombolysed; the reasons are not recorded.
comparison.matching: None. Measured baseline variables did not differ significantly, but co-treatment did: aspirin 49% vs 76% and beta-adrenergic blockade 5% vs 32% in the untreated and treated groups, with no p-values printed; nitroglycerin 85% vs 96% (NS); calcium-channel blockers 17% vs 24% (Table 1, p. 1238). Editors' calculation (Fisher's exact test on counts reconstructed from the percentages and group sizes): aspirin p=0.04, beta-blockade p=0.005.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Contraindications to thrombolysis, certainty of the ECG diagnosis, coronary anatomy, delay from arrival to treatment, hospital and year were not compared; these drive both the treatment decision and outcomes.

outcomes.instruments: Chart review. Serial cardiac isoenzymes every 8 to 12 hours, giving peak CK and CK-MB and time to peak. Complications recorded: heart failure, ventricular tachycardia, supraventricular tachydysrhythmias, bradydysrhythmias, ventricular rupture, septal perforation and death; for thrombolysed patients, clinical evidence of reperfusion and complications attributable to thrombolysis. Major complications were defined as intracerebral haemorrhage or bleeding requiring transfusion (p. 1238).
outcomes.validity_norms: Clinical reperfusion signs (resolution of ECG changes, resolution of chest pain, reperfusion dysrhythmias) were taken from chart notes, and reperfusion was counted when two or more were present, a rule stated only in the Discussion (p. 1239). No angiographic patency or ventricular-function data.
outcomes.operationalization: Safety: major complications attributed to thrombolysis (intracerebral haemorrhage, bleeding requiring transfusion), with minor complications described one by one. Efficacy proxies: peak CK and CK-MB, time to peak, and clinical reperfusion.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p<0.05 for every test (p. 1238). The 10 are the nine comparisons in Table 2 plus lactate dehydrogenase, reported only in the text.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; chart abstraction by site investigators, with treatment known.

analysis.effect_sizes: Major complications attributed to thrombolysis: 0 of 25 (printed 95% CI 0 to 12%); no in-hospital deaths in either group; minor complications in 2 of 25 (a self-limited febrile reaction after streptokinase, not treated; vaginal bleeding without transfusion) (p. 1238). Editors' calculation: 12% equals 3/25, the rule-of-three approximation to a one-sided 95% limit; the exact two-sided 95% interval for 0 of 25 is 0 to 13.7%. Reperfusion signs in 14 of 21 thrombolysed patients with information (67%): resolution of ECG changes 62%, resolution of chest pain 86%, reperfusion dysrhythmias 29% (p. 1238). Not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed (Table 2, p. 1239): median peak CK 1,115 U/L (562–2,669) vs 1,911 (763–3,580); median peak CK-MB 154 (29–283) vs 180 (67–409), unit not given in the table and printed as mg/dL in the abstract; time to peak CK 14.4 vs 13.7 hours (p=0.8); time to peak CK-MB 13.6 vs 11.3 hours (p=0.57); heart failure 7% vs 4%; sustained ventricular tachycardia 2% vs 0%; supraventricular tachycardia 2% vs 8%; bradydysrhythmias 10% vs 12%; deaths 0% vs 0%; all reported as not significant.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted Mann-Whitney U or t tests and chi-square or Fisher's exact tests (p. 1238).
analysis.selective_reporting: Thrombolytic agents and dosing regimens were abstracted but not reported. Lactate dehydrogenase peaks are said not to differ (p. 1238) but appear in no table. Table 1 prints no p-values for the aspirin, calcium-channel-blocker and beta-blocker rows, and the Results text names only nitroglycerin among co-treatments that did not differ (p. 1238), although the Discussion acknowledges more beta-blockade in the treated group (p. 1239).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 25 treated patients, a major-complication rate of up to about 12–14% cannot be excluded (editors' calculation), against the under-2% the authors cite for patients without cocaine use (p. 1239). The authors state the sample is too small to compare complication rates with patients who do not use cocaine (p. 1239).

interpretation_gap.results_show: No intracerebral haemorrhage, transfusion-requiring bleeding or in-hospital death among 25 patients thrombolysed for cocaine-associated infarction at 29 hospitals over 7 years, with two minor complications; no significant differences from 41 untreated ECG-eligible patients in enzyme peaks, time to peak or complications, in groups that differed in co-treatment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that thrombolysis "appears to be safe" (p. 1237), and the Discussion that on this series it would appear safe (p. 1239). Zero events in 25 patients is compatible with a major-complication rate of up to about 12–14% (the paper prints 0 to 12%), so the data exclude only a very high rate; the Limitations put it more accurately, saying the risk does not appear so high as to prohibit use (p. 1239). The series also leaves out the patients most exposed to inappropriate thrombolysis (ST elevation without infarction), whom the authors themselves identify as a problem (p. 1239). On efficacy the abstract is appropriately uncertain, and the Discussion names beta-blocker co-treatment as a possible confounder (p. 1239). The closing management sequence for hospital care (oxygen, intravenous access, benzodiazepines, aspirin and nitroglycerin; then primary angioplasty or thrombolysis for persisting infarction) is the authors' clinical opinion with cited support, not a result of this study (p. 1240).

timeline.event: Bush (ref. 23): report of a patient with cocaine-associated infarction who died of an intracerebral haemorrhage after thrombolysis, the report behind the safety concern (as cited, p. 1239)
Lange et al.: beta-adrenergic blockade potentiated cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction (ref. 5), cited here for the beta-blocker imbalance between groups
This series: 0 of 25 thrombolysed patients had a major complication; combined by the authors with 11 earlier case reports, 1 intracerebral haemorrhage in 36 thrombolysed patients (2.8%)
Single-hospital series with this paper's first author as last author: 6% of 250 patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain met WHO criteria for infarction

replication.where_it_stands: No randomized or adequately sized comparative study of thrombolysis in cocaine-associated infarction is cited; the authors themselves call for prospective studies of ventricular function and arterial patency with standardized co-treatment before widespread use (p. 1240). The safety evidence in this paper is 25 patients plus 11 case reports.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Emergency medicine and toxicology departments at SUNY Stony Brook, Bellevue Hospital Center and the New York City Poison Control Center (NYU), and Mount Sinai Medical Center, Cleveland (p. 1237); 29 participating centres listed (p. 1240). An editorial comment appeared in the same issue (p. 1189, per the note on p. 1237); it was not among the files read.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective registry or trial of patients with cocaine-associated ST-elevation infarction comparing reperfusion strategies with standardized co-treatment, with angiographic patency and ventricular function as outcomes, recording every patient thrombolysed for ST elevation whether or not an infarction is confirmed, and large enough (several hundred treated patients) to estimate major bleeding at rates near 1–2%.

domains.note: Clinicians chose whom to thrombolyse, reasons and contraindications were not recorded, and nothing was adjusted. Measured baseline variables did not differ significantly in small groups, though race came close (83% vs 64% nonwhite; editors' p 0.08–0.15).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Entry required an infarction confirmed after treatment, which excludes patients thrombolysed for ST elevation without infarction; case-finding relied on coding and on chart review limited to patients aged 40 or younger; the number excluded and the unit of analysis are unclear.
Receipt of thrombolysis is recorded in the chart; agents and regimens are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-treatment differed: beta-blockade 32% vs 5% and aspirin 76% vs 49% (editors' p 0.005 and 0.04); the authors note that beta-blockade may have confounded the assessment of efficacy (p. 1239).
Reperfusion information for 21 of 25; completeness of enzyme series and complication records not reported.
Intracerebral haemorrhage and transfusion are hard outcomes; reperfusion was judged from chart notes by unblinded abstractors, and sampling every 8–12 hours limits comparisons of time to peak.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Agents, doses and lactate dehydrogenase data were abstracted but not reported; p-values omitted for co-treatments that differed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I overall follows the worst domains (confounding, selection and co-intervention). For the safety count in the treated group (no major complication in 25) the main problems are selection (patients thrombolysed without infarction are excluded) and imprecision rather than confounding; for the comparison of treated with untreated patients on enzyme peaks and complications, confounding by indication and unequal co-treatment leave the comparison close to uninformative. The card may be cited for what happened to 25 hospital patients thrombolysed for cocaine-associated infarction in 1987–1993 (no major bleeding or intracranial haemorrhage, no deaths, two minor complications) and for how little that observation can exclude; not as evidence that thrombolysis is as safe here as in other patients, or that it does or does not work.

key_findings.finding: Case-finding at 29 US hospitals, 1987–1993: 136 cocaine-associated myocardial infarctions in 130 patients; after excluding those whose initial ECG did not meet TIMI criteria, 25 had received thrombolytic therapy and 41 met the ECG criteria but had not.
key_findings.note: The number excluded, and whether 25 and 41 count patients or infarctions, is not stated.

key_findings.finding: No in-hospital deaths in either group; no intracerebral haemorrhage or bleeding requiring transfusion attributed to thrombolysis (0%, printed 95% CI 0 to 12%); two minor complications: a self-limited febrile reaction after streptokinase, and vaginal bleeding that did not need transfusion.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 0 of 25 has an exact two-sided 95% interval of 0 to 13.7%; 12% is the rule-of-three value (3/25).

key_findings.finding: Clinical evidence of reperfusion (two or more signs) in 14 of 21 thrombolysed patients with charted information (67%): resolution of ECG changes 62%, resolution of chest pain 86%, reperfusion dysrhythmias 29%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy of Thrombolytic Therapy (p. 1238); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 1239)

key_findings.finding: Not thrombolysed (n=41) vs thrombolysed (n=25): median peak CK 1,115 U/L (562–2,669) vs 1,911 (763–3,580); median peak CK-MB 154 (29–283) vs 180 (67–409); time to peak CK 14.4 vs 13.7 hours (p=0.8); time to peak CK-MB 13.6 vs 11.3 hours (p=0.57); none significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy of Thrombolytic Therapy (p. 1238); Table 2 (p. 1239)
key_findings.note: No unit is given for CK-MB in Table 2; the abstract prints mg/dL (p. 1237).

key_findings.finding: In-hospital complications, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: heart failure 7% vs 4%, sustained ventricular tachycardia 2% vs 0%, supraventricular tachycardia 2% vs 8%, bradydysrhythmias 10% vs 12%, death 0% vs 0%; none significant.

Co-treatment, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: nitroglycerin 85% vs 96% (NS), aspirin 49% vs 76%, calcium-channel blockers 17% vs 24%, beta-adrenergic blockade 5% vs 32%; no p-values printed for the last three.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Fisher's exact test on counts reconstructed from the percentages: 20/41 vs 19/25 and 2/41 vs 8/25): aspirin p=0.04, beta-blockade p=0.005.

key_findings.finding: Baseline, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: mean age 38.1 vs 39.8; men 73% vs 88%; nonwhite 83% vs 64%; last cocaine use under 4 hours 39% vs 40% and under 24 hours 81% vs 64%; anterior infarction 49% vs 48%; Q-wave 46% vs 56%; all reported as not significant.
key_findings.note: The abstract describes the groups as similar at p>0.20 (p. 1237); editors' tests on reconstructed counts give p=0.08–0.15 for race depending on the test, and 81% is not a possible share of 41 (33/41 = 80.5%).

key_findings.finding: Adding this series to 11 earlier case reports of thrombolysis for cocaine-associated infarction, the authors count 1 intracerebral haemorrhage (fatal, from a case report) among 36 thrombolysed patients (2.8%).

Limitations stated by the authors: too few patients to compare complication rates with patients who do not use cocaine; difficulty of identifying infarction on the ECG after cocaine (in one cited series 43% met TIMI criteria without infarction); no demonstrated benefit; unstandardized co-treatment, with more beta-blockade in the treated group possibly confounding efficacy.

The authors recommend a cautious policy on thrombolysis in cocaine-associated chest pain with ST elevation and prospective studies with standardized co-treatment before widespread use; their hospital management sequence is opinion supported by other references, not a result of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives median peak CK-MB as 180 vs 154 mg/dL (p. 1237); Table 2 gives no unit (p. 1239), and mg/dL is not a plausible unit for CK-MB; the abbreviation box also defines CK-MB simply as creatine kinase (p. 1237).
reporting_issues.consequence: The CK-MB values cannot be compared with other studies; cite them only as similar between groups.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed 95% CI for 0 of 25 (0 to 12%) is the rule-of-three value; the exact two-sided interval is 0 to 13.7% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either way the data cannot exclude a major-complication rate several times the under-2% the authors cite for patients without cocaine use.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the groups were similar in age, sex, race, risk factors, time since cocaine use and duration of pain at p>0.20 (p. 1237), and Table 1 gives 81% of the untreated group with use in the previous 24 hours (p. 1238). Editors' reconstruction from Table 1 (counts from percentages and group sizes): race (34/41 vs 16/25 nonwhite) gives p=0.08 (chi-square), 0.15 (Yates) or 0.14 (Fisher); sex gives 0.15–0.26 and use within 24 hours 0.14–0.23; and 81% of 41 is not attainable (33/41 = 80.5%, 34/41 = 82.9%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The groups were less similar than the abstract says; with groups of 41 and 25, non-significance says little about comparability.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints no p-values for aspirin (49% vs 76%), calcium-channel blockers or beta-blockade (5% vs 32%), and the Results text lists only nitroglycerin among co-treatments that did not differ (p. 1238).
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' Fisher tests give p=0.04 (aspirin) and p=0.005 (beta-blockade): the groups differed in co-treatment, which the Discussion acknowledges only for beta-blockade (p. 1239).

reporting_issues.issue: 136 infarctions occurred in 130 patients, but the comparison is described in patients without saying how repeat infarctions were handled, and the number excluded for not meeting TIMI criteria is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator and the unit of analysis are unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Lactate dehydrogenase peaks are said not to differ (p. 1238) but appear in no table; the thrombolytic agents and dosing regimens were abstracted (p. 1238) but are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Outcomes and treatment details that were collected cannot be checked.

verification.source_read: PDF of the scanned print pages (version of record), Chest 107(5), pp. 1237–1241 (5 page images; the OCR text layer has errors, so every number was read on 150-dpi renderings; Tables 1–2 checked; p. 1241 holds the last references and an advertisement; no supplement). The editorial comment named on p. 1237 (Chest 107(5), p. 1189) was not among the files read.
